# Recovering business progress after partial failure

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `architecture-saga-compensation` · **Architecture & Distributed Systems** · Catalog level: architect

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S04-Q043](#S04-Q043)

<p>One service has committed successfully but a later service fails. How would you recover the business workflow and make its current outcome visible?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Design observable recovery for a workflow whose services commit independently.</p>

<ul>
<li>Explain the boundary of each local transaction and the intended convergence state.</li>
<li>Distinguish compensation from rollback for a visible business effect.</li>
<li>Choose workflow coordination and trace repeated or failed recovery.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

- [Service interactions under latency and load constraints](architecture-communication.md)
- [Coordinate durable changes with outgoing and incoming events](messaging-outbox.md)

<p>Define what users may observe before all records agree. Establish where transaction protection ends, then examine compensation as a business action. Use a partial failure to test the recovery path before comparing who should coordinate and own the workflow.</p>

<a id="S04-Q040"></a>

### S04-Q040 · Foundation

<p>What does eventual consistency mean for a user observing a business operation? Give an example of temporarily different views and explain what the system must eventually establish.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q040](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q040)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q040](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q040)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain eventual consistency.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Describe a convergence contract and its assumptions. Do not use the label as a substitute for explaining how unfinished work is detected.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Make delayed consistency observable and bounded by an explicit contract.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State the affected records, expected delay and failure assumptions. Do not imply a fixed convergence deadline without a supported design or measurement.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explain which observations may differ and what condition counts as convergence.</li>
<li>Describe detection and recovery when progress stops rather than merely waiting.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Saying the data will become correct eventually without naming the convergence mechanism.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What should the UI show before the views agree?</li>
<li>How would you distinguish expected lag from a stuck workflow?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q039"></a>

### S04-Q039 · Mechanism

<p>Why might one ACID transaction be unavailable or unsuitable across databases owned by independently deployable services? Explain the practical boundary and any assumptions behind your answer.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q039](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q039)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q039](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q039)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Why is a single ACID transaction usually unavailable across independently owned service databases?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>ACID describes database transaction guarantees. Examine coordination across owners and systems rather than assuming a local transaction automatically extends to a remote call.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Reason about transaction scope and distributed coordination constraints.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>The source says usually, not impossible. Establish database/provider support, ownership and availability requirements; verify official capabilities before making a product-specific claim.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Trace which state is protected by each local commit and which remains outside it.</li>
<li>Compare a supported coordination option with its deployment and failure costs.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Claiming cross-database atomic transactions are categorically impossible.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes if both participants support a distributed transaction coordinator?</li>
<li>Which failure would leave the business workflow partially completed?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q042"></a>

### S04-Q042 · Mechanism

<p>What is compensation in a distributed workflow, and how is it different from database rollback? Use a completed business step to explain what can and cannot be reversed.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q042](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q042)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q042](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q042)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What is compensation and why is it not the same as database rollback?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Focus on the business meaning of recovery after a local step has committed. Explain the resulting state rather than assuming every effect has a perfect inverse.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Distinguish business recovery from undoing an uncommitted transaction.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Choose a generic action with visible effects; state which changes are reversible and whether other actors may already have observed them.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Describe a valid recovery state and why it meets the business contract.</li>
<li>Consider repeated or failed compensation and how to inspect its progress.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Calling compensation a rollback that restores every prior observation.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What if the compensation itself fails?</li>
<li>What would you do for an action with no meaningful inverse?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q043"></a>

### S04-Q043 · Failure cases

<p>One service has committed successfully but a later service fails. How would you recover the business workflow and make its current outcome visible?</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q043](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q043)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q043](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q043)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How would you handle a partial failure after one service commits successfully?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Start from the actual committed state, not an assumed all-or-nothing result. Explain the next valid action and how it can be attempted safely.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design recoverable progress after a partial distributed failure.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a generic workflow with independent local transactions; clarify deadlines, reversible actions and who owns recovery.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Trace partial success through a recovery decision and an inspectable state transition.</li>
<li>Test repeated recovery, an unknown remote outcome and recovery failure.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Retrying the whole workflow without checking effects already committed.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What if the later service timed out but might have committed?</li>
<li>When should an operator intervene instead of another automatic attempt?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q041"></a>

### S04-Q041 · Trade-offs

<p>How would you choose between Saga orchestration and choreography for a multi-service workflow? Compare who tracks progress and what happens when a step fails.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q041](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q041)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q041](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q041)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare Saga orchestration and choreography.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>A Saga coordinates a workflow composed of local steps. Explain control and responsibility for the complete workflow, not just whether messages are used.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Compare workflow coordination from ownership and recovery needs.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Choose a generic workflow with local commits; state visibility, team ownership and change requirements. Neither style is assumed to eliminate partial failure.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Trace the happy path and a failed step under both coordination styles.</li>
<li>Explain a condition that changes the choice and how workflow progress is inspected.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Calling choreography fully decoupled without examining implicit event dependencies.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Who decides that the entire workflow has finished?</li>
<li>How would you change a step without breaking an in-progress workflow?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>An order service has committed an order and a stock service has reserved inventory, but a payment call times out. Design the states and decisions for an unknown payment outcome, including who owns investigation, what recovery can repeat safely and how the user sees progress. Do not assume payment failed merely because the call timed out.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Recognizes partial success and distinguishes local rollback from a later recovery action.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Defends valid recovery states, handles unknown outcomes and repeated recovery, and assigns observable workflow ownership.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A Saga diagram without a failure matrix, recovery state transitions or stuck-work detection leaves the guarantee unestablished.</p>
